The 30-day grace period also delays most immediate household charges. The finding therefore documents a confirmed structural reduction in automatic school-meal access, not a verified count of students already going without meals. The district has not established how many students will ultimately pay for meals after applications and direct certification are processed. This finding therefore describes loss of universal automatic access, not a claim that every student outside the 121 CEP schools will lose free meals. The district did not specify in the cited announcement how many total schools or students are outside the 121 CEP campuses, how many students will qualify after applying, how many households will fail to complete applications, or how many students will ultimately begin paying for meals. The 30-day transition may prevent immediate interruption but does not preserve districtwide automatic eligibility. The district does not state how many students attend the non-CEP schools, how many will qualify through direct certification or applications, how many families may fail to complete applications, or how many students will ultimately experience a loss or interruption of free meals. The first-30-days transition policy also means immediate meal denial is not established.
